newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to scrap waterway, N fast-breeder -Jospin.
newsitem.headline: France to scrap waterway, N fast-breeder -Jospin.

text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday he would scrap the fault-prone Superphenix nuclear fast-breeder and drop plans for a waterway to connect the Rhine and Rhone rivers through eastern France.
In his first policy statement to the National Assembly, Jospin described both as too costly and of doubtful value.

"While nuclear industry is a major asset for our country, it cannot be outside democratic rules nor pursue projects whose cost is excessive and whose success is uncertain: this is why the fast-breeder known as Superphenix will be dropped," he said.

The 1,200 megawatt, 60-billion franc ($10.5 billion) Superphenix plant, 51 percent owned by state utility Electricite de France, with Italy's ENEL and a Dutch-German-Belgian consortium as partners, was built 20 years ago near the Alpine town of Grenoble to produce more plutonium than it consumed.

But it has been on line for only 30 months and fed the electricity grid for only 10 months. The government downgraded it in 1994 to a research reactor working at reduced power as a tool of research into dAuposing of nuclear waste.

The group Europeans against Superphenix, who had described the plant as a dangerous dinosaur, hailed its announced closure as "the victory of David over Goliath" and "a historical date among great ecological battles".

It was a success for Greens leader Dominique Voynet, who became environment minister after the left's victory in June 1 elections. She had denounced the reactor as "stupid financial waste" and was determined to scrap the proposed waterway.
Supporters of Superphenix have warned of the high cost of an early closure for majority owner Electricite de France, and of dire losses of jobs and tax income for the region.
A disputed 1995 government study said it would cost up to 20 billion francs ($3 billion) to close the plant two decades ahead of the scheduled date of 2020.

The reactor was due to restart this month after shutting down six months ago because of more faults. But the Council of State, France's top administrative court, cancelled its 1994 authorisation to operate as a research reactor.
The council ruled that the procedure for transforming the power plant into a research prototype was flawed and required a new public inquiry.
Former conservative prime minister Alain Juppe was believed to have wanted to keep the plant operating. But his defeat in the June 1 elections sounded Superphenix's death knell.

The Rhone-Rhine Waterway to connect northern Europe to the Mediterranean, was due to be completed by 2010 by widening an existing narrow waterway to allow 4,400 tonnes barges through the Doubs valley.

Jospin said he wanted to avoid embarking into cumbersome projects whose value was outweighed by cost and environmental nuisance. "This is the case of the proposed wide Rhone-Rhine Waterway that the government has decided to end," he said.
Part of the waterway has already been built but the projected cost for the remaining 200 kms (120 miles) had risen from 17 billion francs ($2.9 billion) to 28 billion francs ($4.8 billion).

Its main backer was former prime minister Raymond Barre, the mayor of Lyon on the Rhone river. Electricite de France, which was to contribute to the financing by paying taxes on its hydroelectrical dams on the Rhone, was increasingly reluctant.

The previous environment minister Corinne Lepage had slowed down the project which she called pharaonic. Britain's Prince Philip, head of the World Wildlife Fund, visited the site in 1995 and said it would harm the environment.
